identity.title: The OVCA1-A2BR-ROS axis drives gastric cancer aggressiveness and identifies an actionable precision target.

content.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Gastric cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, underscoring the urgent need for novel therapeutic targets. Ovarian cancer gene 1 (OVCA1) has been implicated as a tumor suppressor in various malignancies; however, its clinical relevance and mechanistic role in gastric cancer progression remain poorly defined. METHODS: We assessed OVCA1 expression in a large clinical cohort (n = 616) and performed prognostic analyses (n = 417). The functional consequences of OVCA1 knockdown, overexpression, and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout were evaluated in gastric cancer cell lines. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic profiling, together with in vivo xenograft and peritoneal metastasis models, were utilized to elucidate the downstream molecular mechanisms. Furthermore, the therapeutic potential of the selective adenosine A2B receptor (A2BR) antagonist BAY-545 was tested both in vitro and in vivo. RESULTS: Low OVCA1 expression was significantly associated with aggressive clinicopathological features and shorter patient survival. Functionally, OVCA1 loss promoted proliferation, invasion, and cell-cycle progression, whereas its overexpression reversed these phenotypes. Multi-omics integration linked OVCA1 deficiency to purine metabolism remodeling, marked by CD73/NT5E upregulation and selective elevation of the adenosine receptor A2BR. OVCA1-deficient tumors exhibited increased ROS accumulation and upregulation of MMP14 and VEGF. Notably, pharmacological A2BR inhibition with BAY-545 effectively mitigated the enhanced malignancy of OVCA1-knockout cells, suppressed ROS production, and significantly reduced tumor growth and peritoneal dissemination in vivo. CONCLUSION: Our findings identify a novel OVCA1-A2BR-ROS axis contributing to gastric cancer aggressiveness. Given that A2BR blockade robustly reverses OVCA1-loss-associated phenotypes, this study supports A2BR as a potential actionable target and provides a preclinical rationale for its further evaluation in OVCA1-deficient gastric cancer.
